utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Please be kind enough to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you hearing me in a thank that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, for the Prosecution, Anna Richterova and Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to. Madam Registrar should I announce for Thursday or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested to you that the Thursday sitting it's now possible for us to sit in the morning rather than the afternoon, if that is okay with the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. We have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any problems, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I appreciate that, Your Honour, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you both for your cooperation. So Thursday we will be sitting in this courtroom, however. All right? Good. So, yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you were advised yesterday by Ms. Korner I wish to make an application for protective measures for the coming witness, which is 7.135. And if I may to ask for private session just for reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session for a while. No objection? We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session. Any preliminaries, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the memorandum has been submitted and filed and I received a copy of it from the registry this morning so I know it's been filed and you should have it, the one that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do have some preliminaries. One, I will defer because Ms. Korner is not here and I wouldn't want to speak about it until she is. The first one is this: Rule 53 bis requires personal service on the accused of an indictment. The rule says that must be done by giving him a certificated copy prepared in accordance with requirements of Rule 47(G). Rule 47(G) provides that the certificated copy shall be in the language of the accused. I don't believe that the new indictment, which was filed yesterday afternoon, has been served upon Mr. Brdjanin in accordance with the requirements of Rule 53 bis and Rule 47(G) and my question is what is the Chamber's intention with regard to requirements of the rule in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to 53?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rule 53 bis requires personal service on the accused in accordance with Rule 47(G) which requires it be in the language of the accused. Then my follow-up question would be is it necessary that he enter a new plea to the new indictment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I think we went through yesterday and 53 bis does not -- seems to me to be referring to the original -- to the very first indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it can't be that the rules provide that the only indictment that has to be served on the defendant is the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rule says service of the indictment shall be affected personally on the accused at the time the accused is taken into custody or as soon as reasonably practicable thereafter. So if we are referring to the point in time of taking into custody, it is obvious to me that, without prejudice to any further submissions that you may make and on which we are open, but it seems to me that 53 bis refers to the very first, the original indictment. In other words, the one which needs to be served on him upon being taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour should the trial proceed on that indictment, if that's being the one that's served on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because then there is another rule which makes it possible for the indictment to be amended. Even after the Trial Chamber as such has been composed and the trial started which we went through yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position, then, Your Honour that the amended indictment does not need to be served upon the accused in his language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position of the Trial Chamber is that you have invoked Rule 53 bis and I'm telling that you Rule 53 bis does not seem to apply on the face of it because it refers to the indictment which needs to be served at the time the accused is taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, apart from Rule 53 bis let me simply say that it is my considered belief that the purpose of Rule 53 bis or any rule similar to it is to advise the defendant in his own language of what it is he's charged with and to enable him to assist his counsel in defending himself. And so whether it's Rule 53 bis or just some general concept of due process, it seems to me that Mr. Brdjanin should have in his possession a B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman, okay. The Chamber -- you may sit down. The Chamber, having heard Mr. Ackerman's submission for the application of Rule 53 bis, namely to the effect of the need to have a copy of the new indictment -- new amended indictment on the accused, and his further request, basically a repetition of the request made yesterday, that his client be given time to enter pleas on the new indictment, the Trial Chamber has seen Rule 53 bis and Rule 50(A)(iii), which makes Rule 53 bis applicable mutatis mutandis to an amended indictment, orders that a copy of the amended indictment, as per yesterday's decision of this Chamber, be served on the accused without delay, in a language that he understands. Service will be effected personally on the accused, who, however, is not being granted time to file any -- to file -- to enter pleadings as requested by him yesterday and today, the reason being that -- which was specifically referred to yesterday in the oral decision given by this Chamber -- namely that the amended indictment does not include any new charges and the amendments effectively do not in any way affect his standing before this Trial Chamber as an accused person. Yes. Any further demands?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there was a misunderstanding. I don't believe I have ever asked that Mr. Brdjanin actually be permitted to plead to the new indictment. I raised the issue this morning as to what Your Honour's position was with regard to that but I didn't state my own position. My own position, if I had had an opportunity to state it, would have been that I think it's unnecessary because the indictment has not changed significantly. But I was wondering if Your Honour might feel that it was required by the rules. That's the only reason I raised that and I don't think I raised it at all yesterday. Yesterday I was talking about Rule 72 and my ability to file motions directed to the indictment under Rule 72. In any event you've dealt with it and I'm satisfied with how you've dealt with it and I don't think that the requirement that he be served with the indictment should in any way affect the calling of the witnesses today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and I hope the continuation of this trial. I don't see why it should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the last thing I would expect to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Secondly, and this came to me in the middle of the night Your Honour, I'm making no objection, it's just something that I wonder about, and maybe the Chamber should wonder about it. Judge Hunt, as I recall, ruled at one point with regard to an amended indictment on a query by Mr. Pitron that an amended indictment completely supplants the prior indictment and the prior indictment is of no further force and effect. I don't know that there is any jurisprudence of this Tribunal beyond that minor statement by Judge Hunt with regard to that. The problem that occurred to me in my sleep was, are there now two indictments pending against Mr. Brdjanin, the new one filed yesterday and the one in which he's charged jointly with General Talic, or is there just the one indictment and if so, then what is the indictment pending against General Talic? I don't know the answer to those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not something that you alone thought about it, and I can tell you here off the cuff what my feelings are. Number 1, if you go back -- it's true that Judge Hunt decide what you just stated. If you go back to the December 2001 decision or November 23rd -- sorry, 23rd November, 2001 decision given by Judge Hunt as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case until then, before I stepped in instead of him, you will recall that what he did was he directed the Prosecution to -- the Prosecution had sought to amend the indictment and Judge Hunt, if I remember well, directed the Prosecution to represent a fourth amended indictment. At the time you already had a fourth indictment. And what remained was a fourth amended indictment, and that's what we had until yesterday. Yesterday, if you noticed, I tried to avoid at all costs referring to a fifth indictment. So what we have before us, I think, is still a fourth further amended indictment, which excludes now Mr. Talic as one of the co-accused, but I don't think we have a new indictment. Any way, we are open for any submissions you may have in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This morning, I received a certificated, signed document called the Prosecutor's fifth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can't be the fifth amended indictment because there was never a fifth indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, fifth I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there was never a fifth indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only reading you what it says on the front of the indictment, Your Honour. It says, "Prosecutor's fifth amended indictment." I'm not making that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you, Ms. Sutherland, would you take this up with Ms. Korner if necessary to have a correction? Because there was never a fifth indictment. There was a fourth amended indictment. That's what we started with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was entitled the fifth amended indictment because it's the fifth time that the original indictment has been amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There it was a fourth amended indictment and then there was a corrected fourth amended indictment and the one we have been proceeding under was the corrected fourth amended indictment until yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, we will look into this. We'll look into this. It's not going to change the substance of what your client is charged within any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will look into this and Madam Registrar -- Madam Registrar, could you please locate for me all the indictments that we have had so far? Because what Ms. Sutherland has just stated may be the practice has been indictment, then the first time it's amended it becomes the first amended indictment, but it could be like that. I don't know because -- I don't know what the practice has been so far here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The order came out -- the decision of Judge Hunt of the 23rd of November asking us to file a corrected version which is what we filed on the 10th of December, 2001. So it was the corrected version of the fourth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, this would be the fifth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the position we took was because this was the fifth amendment to the original indictment, that's what we called it. But I will discuss it with Ms. Korner in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We will go into that but please do let me have, by the end of today or tomorrow morning, it's not that urgent a matter, I understand, Mr. Ackerman, we can deal with it but in any case -- in any case, we will come back to you on it tomorrow. If it is as you say, then obviously it should be the fifth amended indictment. I was acting under the presumption that the system adopted here is completely different. It is completely different in my country any way, so... All right? Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I wanted to discuss at some length the Randal matter this morning but I'm going to defer that because Ms. Korner is not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could perhaps Ms. Gustin send an e-mail to Ms. Korner telling her what time, towards the end of the sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Doesn't even have to be today. It can be tomorrow it. It's not an urgent matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's communicate this to Ms. Korner and then perhaps during the break, you can liaise and see when it's convenient to both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for Ms. Korner to be here, I don't care when it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin will be doing precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The final thing I wanted to bring to Your Honour's attention was this and it would have flowed from what I was going to say about the Randal matter but it is this: There came a time in this case when Milka Maglov was suspended and I explained to Your Honour at that point that that could cause serious problems for Mr. Brdjanin's defence because Ms. Maglov was the person most familiar with all of the documents in the case and that I was relying quite heavily on her for that. We have muddled along since she left, one way or another. We then got Mr. Trbojevic here as Mr. Brdjanin's new co-counsel under a very difficult circumstance, because here he is in the middle of a trial, in an ongoing trial, and faced with the proposition of trying to become familiar with all of the thousands of pages of documents in this case, with what I believe must be at least 100 hours of video tapes and maybe another 30 or 40 hours of audiotapes. I just have not measured them to see how many hours of material there is there that Ms. Maglov was familiar with that Mr. Trbojevic now must become familiar with. Yesterday, Mr. Trbojevic received a letter from the registry saying that they were not paying him for several of the hours that he had claimed during the last month because they didn't feel it was necessary since we were in court such a short period of time, and to me that's just an unacceptable situation. Earlier on in this case, Your Honour might remember from reading earlier documents in this case, there was a time when a similar situation occurred and I requested of Judge Hunt that a matter be deferred because my investigators in Banja Luka had used up the hours that they were allotted for that month and that it be deferred until the next month and Judge Hunt ruled that that was -- that was a perfectly appropriate request and in fact delayed a deadline over into the next month so that they could work on the hours that had been allotted for them that month. If it's going to continue to be the position of the registry that we are only permitted to work what amounts to roughly eight hours a day on this case, then I suggest to Your Honour that what we should do is when we come to that point in the month when we have used up our hours, advise the Trial Chamber and adjourn until the following month because I don't think it is appropriate for this Tribunal to ask us to engage in involuntary servitude and to perform work for this Tribunal for which we can not be recompensed. I say that in the context of the proposition that I probably bill the Tribunal for about two-thirds of the hours I actually put in because I work almost constantly on this case. I do almost nothing else. But to do what happened yesterday, when the number of hours requested didn't even approach the maximum that's allowed, my recollection of it is that Mr. Trbojevic requested payment for 97 hours and was not granted that. He was only granted 90 because they felt the work he did was unnecessary. And I have already moved one time to dismiss this case on the grounds that if the Tribunal cannot provide sufficient resources to properly defend the case, then it should not go forward and I'm prepared to do it again if something can't be done about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any comments, Ms. Sutherland or Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber directs that this part of today it's proceedings, that is the relative transcript, be communicated to what's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Christian Rohde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Christian Rohde, who is being also directed to enter a memo in regard. And we will take it up from there, after I have heard the other side of the story. So can we bring in the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want it to say that I dislike raising matters like this in open court but there comes a time when it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman you would be very stupid if you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you feel you are being hampered, what baffles me is bringing in Mrs. Maglov in the picture in the beginning because she has got nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She does have something to do with it only in this regard, Your Honour, the burden placed upon Mr. Trbojevic to get to the place that she was at in a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's been here for quite sometime now so... Anyway, and the Maglov thing is being taken care of and you should expect a decision on whether there are going to be contempt proceedings Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pretty soon. In fact, discussing the topic within the next days, with, first, the legal officer who has prepared me a memo and then with the two Judges later on. So can we proceed with the witness? Mr. Usher and Registrar, please do take care since we are putting into effect the protective measures and this is Courtroom II, I understand that no -- no one should be allowed in that -- in the gallery, in the private gallery, but they can of course follow it from downstairs. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. You are going to give evidence, to testify in this trial, against Radoslav Brdjanin, and according to the rules, I need to call upon you to enter a solemn declaration that you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth in the course of your testimony. The declaration is contained -- the text of the declaration is contained in the piece of paper that you're going to be given and you are kindly asked to read it out aloud and that would be your solemn undertaking to this Tribunal to tell us the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. So as the Presiding Judge in this trial, and on behalf of the other two Judges, Judge Janu and Judge Taya I should like to welcome you to this Tribunal and thank you for having accepted to come forward and give evidence. This morning, we were informed that you had asked for some protective measures to be put in place, namely your anonymity, in other words you will not be referred to by your name and family name, but by a nom de plume, a number we have given you and you are now witness number BT-77. That's how you will be referred to in the course of your testimony. You also asked for your anonymity to be preserved in another manner, that is by having your figure distorted. In other words, I don't know what you have on the screen now but if you are on video, you will see how others are going to see you. They are not going to see your face at any time, they are just going to see those squares, and that's what we call facial distortion. That's the second protective measure that you asked for and that this Tribunal also with the consent and approval of the defence has decided to grant you. The procedure here is a very simple one. You will be first asked questions by the Prosecution and as I understand it, the officer from the Prosecution that will handle the examination-in-chief is Madam Richterova, who is sitting in the centre to your right, and then once the examination-in-chief is concluded, the Defence team will conduct what is known, what we refer to as cross-examination. In other words, they will put to you questions as well. There is no difference essentially as far as you are concerned between questions asked by the Prosecution and questions asked by the Defence. You have a duty to answer all questions irrespective of where they are coming from or irrespective of who is putting those questions to you. In other words you will not be allowed to become hostile either to the Prosecution or to the Defence simply because you don't like who is putting the questions to you or you don't like the question. You will be protected, of course, and the Tribunal will not allow any questions that have the potentiality of harassing you or of putting you in discomfort unduly, so Madam Richterova, you may proceed now with your first question. Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness, I will ask usher to show you a piece of paper on which is your name and please only confirm whether it is your name. Do not read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Will you show it to Mr. Ackerman, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit under seal, number P1104.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were born and you live in a village of Prhovo. How many inhabitants had village of Prhovo in the time where you lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: There were about 60 houses with about 200 villagers so there was a total of about 60 houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness new Exhibit P1105 which is the map of Prhovo, let us say Prhovo overview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the way, Witness, I forgot to tell you that I'm very sorry that you had stay waiting in the room outside before you were brought in this courtroom. The reason is not because we were ignoring you. The reason is that we had some urgent business to attend to, procedural matters, and I'm sorry that we had to keep you waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is P?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This is P1105. Maybe we need a little bit more clear picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you cannot see it on the screen, turn to your right and point, please, where is your village on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, the witness pointed at the village of Prhovo. We may leave this map on the ELMO because we will need it later on. I would like to focus today on the events which occurred on or about 1st of June but only briefly. Can you tell us, in 1992, the first half of 1992, how was the life in your village? And was there any change during this period which would struck you -- which would -- which you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We felt a change from the 26th onwards and around June the 1st. Before the 26th of May, everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was change around 26th of May. In which way? What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: There was shooting around the village, in the woods close to the village. Then we sent a sort of delegation to Plamenica. This was a Serb village, to see what was going on, to find out whether anybody was going to attack us. So three of our men went in that delegation and they went to the house of Milan and Branko Brankovic in this village. It was their house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you speak a little bit slower? We will come to everything. Just for the purposes of translation. So please slow down. You said you sent a delegation of three men to village of Brankovici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was it Plamenica? Yeah, you stated to the village --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: It's a village on the map, the actual village is called Gomile but that is where the Brankovics' house is. It's here on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it's on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I cannot see the village Brankovici itself so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Brankovici is the name, Milan Brankovic is the person that he was -- that was visited at this initial period, and later on by three other persons that are mentioned in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to the village -- the delegation went to the village of Plamenica in the houses of these people who were called Brankovici? Do you remember who were these representatives who went to the village of Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Camil Medanovic, Sefik Medanovic, and Tehvid Osmanovic. They were the ones who went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when they returned and what happened after they returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They were accompanied by Branko Brankovic and Milanko Popovic. I recognised them. They went after them. I was up on a tree, in the woods, and then myself and Enes Medanovic went to the village to let them know but we had to go through the woods. We couldn't go through the field so that they wouldn't see us. When we got to the village the army had already reached the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw these three men accompanied by these two Brankovics. And then you state that you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Popovic and Brankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you stated the army arrived. Did you also see army coming behind this group of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: By the time we got to the village from the woods, the army was already there. I didn't see when soldiers got there but when we got to the village, it was full of soldiers, the village itself and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are talking about soldiers, are you able to describe what did they wear? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I recognised Milanko Popovic and Branko Brankovic. They were the only people whom I knew. I didn't recognise any of the others because they were masked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they had masks, what kind of masks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They had transparent socks on their heads and they also had those soldiers' ski caps, ski masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "army," did they wear some kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the army came to your village, what happened? And we are talking about this 26th of May. So what happened at that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They gathered all the villagers that they found in the village into two groups in Medanovici near the shop and the other group was gathered in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after they gathered these people, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They asked the villagers to hand over their weapons and said that nothing would happen to them if they handed the weapons over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it the first time you heard about surrender of weapons or were there some previous announcements asking for surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I heard that then for the first time in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did the people in the village surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. All of those who had them and who happened to be in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give the weapons to these soldiers or where did they -- where did they get them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The soldiers told us to throw those weapons into a pile. So that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they take them away with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know. They probably did. They didn't leave them with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any receipt for surrender of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, did you personally, have some weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I didn't but my father did, because he was in the police reserves before the war. So they had taken away the uniform, but the pistol remained and he had a permit for it, a licence for it, and I handed it over to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you surrender the weapons, what did the soldiers do? Did they leave the village? Did they search the village? Or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They told us to go, to follow a certain road, both in the Medanovici group and in the Hadzici group, they put us all on one road. And they told us to look towards Hadzici, towards Hamdo Hadzici's house and they said it takes years to build a house, and it takes a very little time to burn it, and then they torched it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they torched the house of Hamid Hadzic, what did -- what the army did then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We were standing on the road. We couldn't see what the soldiers were doing in the village. They were beating people. I was standing on the road with the women and children. There was some other men there, older men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the army stay in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: About two or three hours, four hours at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to state that after maximum of four hours, the soldiers left your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 26 of May, did soldiers return to your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. They didn't come to the village. We didn't see them. We worked normally for three or four days at the end of May, and then we saw that Pudin Han and Krasulje were burning but in the village we did our usual duties, we cut the grass and so on. Nobody touched us for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these two or three days, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then the soldiers came back to the village again. I think it was in the afternoon. And they beat us. Before that, they threw a grenade which fell to -- into a field called Dolovi. It was in front of the village. So it didn't set anything in the village on fire because it fell on the outskirts of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was about 3 days after the first appearance of the soldiers so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was approximately the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, because we weren't really able to think about anything else other than how to save ourselves. We were constantly living in fear about when somebody would come and kill you. But this happened at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that these soldiers came to your village again and they beat people and throw this hand grenades. What else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. When the grenade fell we went to Vahid Medanovic's house to hide, and after about half an hour, we could hear some vehicles arriving into the village. Then Gane Mesic and I went to see what this vehicle was, who was it that was coming, and we saw soldiers and they told us to stop, and we stood still. Then they asked us, "Where are the others?" And I told them that they were in Vahid's house. And then they told me to go and call everybody to come, and to gather by Karanfil Osmanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will return quickly to these soldiers. Were they the same soldiers as on that previous occasion or were they some different soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who the soldiers were the first time or the second time. They were masked and we had to look down. We weren't allowed to look at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was on this particular occasion, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: JNA camouflage uniforms and they were also civilians among them. I think I saw a few men in civilian clothes. But they also had masked heads so I couldn't see who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who wore camouflage uniforms, would you be able to say whether they wore some insignias on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I noticed that they had white ribbons on their soldiers -- on their shoulders. They were tied to their shoulders but not all of them had those ribbons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I will return where we finished before. So you were -- you were ordered to gather in front of the Karanfil Osmanovic's house, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were in front of this house, what did you see? What was happening around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I saw a yellow truck, it was a civilian truck, and Hamdo Islamagic was brought in this truck and he was all bloodied and his clothes were torn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he was brought in the truck. Was he lying on that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. No. They were dragging him on the road, along the road. They were dragging him on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him when you drag him in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and repeat your answer, slowly, for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. Later, we found him, we found him dead. He was killed. And now he's buried in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they dragged in Hamdija Islamagic, what happened further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They brought us all before Karanfil's house. Then they beat certain people, and called out their names. They called them to come out. And then when they called these persons out, then I could hear a shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said they called people out, what do you mean? The people who were already gathered in front of this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. The people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall names of those people who were called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Not all of them but I remember Reuf Osmanovic, Isak Mesic, Hasim Hadzic, and Camil Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you could hear a shot. Where did you hear these shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Close by, in the village, very close to us, because we heard them say, "run," and then we heard shots that were being fired after these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "We heard them say, "run," whom they said "run"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The soldiers told those people that they had called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you refer to those people who were called out and you were stating their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you heard these shots, do you know what happened to these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: When we started towards Peci, we saw those men lying on the ground dead next to the road. They were lying on the ground. They had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will return again to the moment when these people were called out and you stated that later you heard these shots. What happened then in the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they called me out, they called out my first and last name, for me it to come out of the line and they told me to take off my jacket and to throw down my documents in front of the garage. I did so and I started and then a soldier, I don't know him, he must have been a school friend of mine, and he said, "Don't hurt him." So they didn't kill me and I went back in line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were back in line. And what at this point, what did the soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they said that all the men should form a line, two by two, and head towards Peci and so all of us who were there did form this column. Most of us were there, except for two or three men who were in hiding. And then we started off towards Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to women and children? Were they allowed to stay in the Prhovo or were they taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The women, when we started for Peci, the women stayed behind in a group and then we set off to Peci. However, there are some meadows of ours down there and a vehicle of theirs got stuck. It was a civilian Ford, I remember. Then they told to us stop near this puddle, this mud, and they told to us stop there and that five of us should come out and drag the car out of the mud. So I, Osme Jusic, Hilmo Jusic, Nedzad Jusic, and Medanovic Sulejman came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Medanovic Sulejman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to for the purpose of interpretation, this Medanovic, what was -- what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Sulejman Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because before, we didn't get the name. So you -- excuse me. So you were ordered to drag the car out of the mud. Did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they told us to go back in line and then they opened fire on us and they killed Hilmo Jusic, Osme Jusic, and Nedzad Jusic and Sulejman was just wounded in the eye. I, thank God, was not hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these three men were killed. What happened --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them? Did you take them with you or did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. They stayed behind. We had to continue on our way to Peci. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And they killed a soldier of theirs on the same occasion, whether this was by mistake, I don't know, but anyway, one of their soldiers was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So. And what happened after they found out that one of their soldiers was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then I heard Marko Adamovic ordering everything to be burnt in the village and for everybody to be killed, for no one to be left alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said Marko Adamovic ordered everything to be burned down, you didn't mention this name before. Did -- who was Marko Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: He must have been the commander of their unit, the unit that was in our village. I personally didn't know him but I heard later on from people who knew him that it was Marko Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after -- I will rephrase it. You said that Marko Adamovic ordered to burn the village. What happened? Could you -- what did you hear? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: It is quite close by and we just heard an explosion and shooting in the village, but later, we learnt that they had killed the people there. We couldn't see anything because we were on the road to Peci and we couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were on the road to Peci so you left Prhovo, you stop when the car was stuck in that puddle. Where did you go further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then we headed on towards Peci. We came to an intersection, there is a road turning to Sokolovo and another to Peci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I ask the usher that I think it is still on the ELMO. I don't know whether it is switched on or not. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could use the marker and show the way from Prhovo to Peci, how did they go? And if --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Here, there is an intersection to the right it leads to Sokolovo and to the left it is Peci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't we give him a coloured pen, preferably in red or -- no, no, something much thinner than that. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There are some markers so one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he marks on the map the route that was followed. In this march from Prhovo to Peci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the main road. This is the main road leading to Peci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with here. Where the truck was stuck and you were asked to pull it out of the mud, where was that? Where would that be? Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about half a kilometre from Prhovo towards Peci, about half a kilometre or one kilometre from the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Start drawing, sketching on that map, please, the route which you believe you followed from Prhovo to Peci. Just draw it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the turning for Sokolovo and then the road goes on to Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started from Prhovo so please start from Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: This is towards Peci and here is the turning to Sokolovo. Left -- to the left is Sisarice a Serbian village and to the right is Sokolovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the village of Prhovo on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go from the Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I can see Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you go from Prhovo to that crossroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please, can you draw the way where you march on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be so kind and make a cross at the place where the car got stuck in the puddle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: One kilometre from Prhovo towards the intersection of the road leading to Peci. I think it was about one kilometre from the village along the road towards this intersection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It is probably -- if we take this map, it will be probably in the middle between Prhovo and the crossroad, is it correct to state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: It's closer to Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly because the scale, as I have it at least on it this map, the distance between Prhovo and the crossroad is easily of two kilometres. So I think what you are suggesting, Madam Richterova, should be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you be so kind and make a cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him point the cross where he thinks --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you think the car got struck? Please make a cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: It was closer to our village than to this junction in the road. This is somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, if it was nearer to the village than the junction, why are you putting the cross right on the junction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put it closer to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm confused by the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's where the village is. Okay? Where you're pointing now. So where was the truck stuck? If you say it was nearer to the village than to the junction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So could I ask you to put a CR there, please, underneath, write the letters CR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we will go on with your description of the journey from Prhovo to Peci. You said that you reach the crossroad, and what happened at this crossroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They killed two or three men there, but I couldn't really see because we had to have our heads bowed and our hands like this behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said that someone, somebody was killed, why do you think that someone was killed? Could you hear something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We could hear the shots and when we returned to the column, we saw that these men were missing. Sometime you're in the front, sometimes in the middle, sometimes in -- at the end of the column. You run around to avoid getting beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from this crossroad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We were heading towards Peci and there is a small hamlet called Sisarice we stopped there for a while. We recognised Jule Sisarice [phoen] and Brano Sisarice [phoen]. And there were some Serbian women there too. And they cursed our balija mothers saying that we should all be killed and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from here, did you go on towards the village of Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. Then we continued towards Peci and we arrived in a field, just as we were approaching this area called polje, fields, and they told us all to stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you stopped, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We were ordered to take off everything from the waste up and our shoes and to form a group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were ordered to put your -- take your shoes off. Where did you put these shoes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We put them under a tree, right next to us. There was this tree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you take off your shoes, your shirts, jackets, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they ordered us to form a group and we -- when we had formed this group, then they opened fire, bursts of fire, at us and we all threw ourselves to the ground, both those who were dead and those who were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did shooting last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Well, not long, not even half a minute, just a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they stop shooting, what followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We all fell to the ground and then I heard somebody say, "All those who were alive were to stand up," because they would check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stand up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Those of us who were alive, we all got up. There were 14 of us. And then they checked to see those who were dead. They would shoot at them and trample on them with their boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were 14 of you. What happened with 14 of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they said, as if there were two too many, because if only 12 of us remain alive, they -- we cannot take our revenge on them. I don't know what they meant by revenge. And then they took out Senad Hadzic and Ismet Mesic, because they were the youngest amongst us. Ismet was standing in front of me and Senad right behind me. And they took them out and one soldier killed them by firing from his pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there were only 12 of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recollect how many of you left Prhovo? I know that you probably cannot state exact number but do you remember approximately how many of you there were in Prhovo who left for Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: There were about 30 of us, over 30. I cannot give you the exact number because I was right in front and you had to bow down your head and put your hands behind your head like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, all these people, except 12 of you, died during the march from Prhovo to Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Some were killed in the village and there were others who were killed on the road, and I couldn't look. You were on the run all the time so as not to get beaten because they were beating us all the time with the butts of their guns, with wires, with sticks, with poles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were 12 of you and where were you taken from this field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We left this Polje area to Dom which was a kind of centre of the cooperative and the post office on the road from Kljuc to Sanski Most. It is about halfway between Kljuc and Sanski Most and the village was called Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to take back your shoes and your jackets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no. We were bare foot and naked from the waist up. All these things were left behind. And later on, we found all these things, all our footwear tied up in a sack after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were taken in front of so-called Dom in Peci. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They tied our hands with wire and string and then they told us that the next morning they would slaughter six and kill the other six with bullets so they ordered us to lie down next to an electricity pole. Then we lay down and they beat us and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive at any point some food or water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, nothing, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long did you stay in this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We arrived there about 8.00 in the evening or 7.30. Any way, night was falling and we stayed there until the morning, about 9.30, 10.00. So we spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Around midnight or 1.00 a.m., I don't know exactly, Sulejman Medanovic died. He was an older man, he was a pensioner any way, and he died from the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you stayed there until the morning. What happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, a van arrived, a civilian van, and transferred us to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: In Kljuc, we arrived in front of the MUP building, the police, and the driver went inside to the police station and, when he returned, he said there was no more room in there, everything was full, and then they transported us to the elementary school in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this elementary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Nikola Mackic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were taken in this Nikola Mackic elementary school. How long did you stay in this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We arrived there around 11.00 and we were in the school for interrogation. They asked us who had weapons and who was a combatant, and after they interrogated us they took us into the gymnasium, the gym of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this gymnasium was still within this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. It belonged to the school. It was used for physical education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything which would struck your attention in this gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: When we entered the gym, I saw that there were a lot of people there and that there were blood stains on the walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask about this blood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, I didn't dare ask anything. We just had to look down and sit on the ground and face the wall with our hands behind our heads like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so I will repeat my previous question. How long did you stay in this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We were in the school from about 11.00 until the evening about 7.00 or 8.00, until the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this day in it the school, did you receive any meal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you receive some water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the school, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Then they told us to come out of the school in a line, two by two, and in front of the municipality building, their buses were waiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so were you put on these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken by these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They took us to an elementary school in Sitnica, a Serbian village, into a hall there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Sitnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. Five or six days. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many men or how many people were together with you in Sitnica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I think there were more than 500 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sitnica -- in the Sitnica school, where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We slept in this hall on the ground again, though you couldn't really sleep because there were so many people. The area was small and any way, we were beaten up, half dead, so no one can really sleep or even sit from the bruises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While in Sitnica, did you receive any meal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: We would get a sandwich, a small sandwich, every 24 hours, some bread and salami.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While in Sitnica, were you told why -- why you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no one said anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken from Sitnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: From Sitnica, we set off on foot towards the camp in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said on foot. Did you have -- did you receive back your shoes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no. We were all barefoot and with no clothes from the waist up, so when we arrived at Manjaca, our feet were bleeding from the stones and the grass.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So now we can have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will have 25 minutes' break, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you a document which is Exhibit P947. I show you this document yesterday but did you see it before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution received this document from Sanski Most AID in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure whether we need to put it on the ELMO for Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For Mr. Brdjanin. So if we have a spare copy so we can put it on the ELMO. And if we could put B/C/S version on the ELMO. Yes, exactly. We do not know who is the author of this document, and if you could have a look on the page 1, on the left hand top, you can see the words "name and father's name." Can you have a look on this list and can you see -- no, I cannot ask this question because he is a protected witness. I will ask another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see at the end, and there is a word "napomena" in English, "Note." And it says --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we take it off the ELMO, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a note stating, "In fighting with army and police members, in addition to the above named who were captured in the zone of combat operation and imprisoned, the following persons were killed." Can you see this note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this note is followed by names. Did you have opportunity to read these names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people killed in fighting with army and police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. There was no fighting there by the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were these people killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They were killed, some people were killed in the village, some people were killed on the road, and some people were killed in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "in the field" do you mean the field near to Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go to the private session just for this one document on which are some information relevant for this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection? Yes. We go into private session for a while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we can take away this document. Now I want to show the witness four documents which relate to exhumations. First document is P1106. Which is disclosure number 9.476.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My only question is: Are you aware that there was an exhumation in the village of Prhovo in May, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document states that the location of the exhumation -- of the exhumation place was -- and I will read the document, "These civilian victims, inhabitants of the village of Prhovo were buried in a mass grave located in a valley on land belonging to Karanfil Osmanovic right next to the dirt road that runs through the village." Is Karanfil Osmanovic the person in front of whose house you were gathered before you left for Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stated that you were aware about this exhumation. Did you participate in the exhumation itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because I'm employed in a company and I wasn't able to go. The company wouldn't allow me to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you participate in the identification process of the people who were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P1107, it's a document which was disclosed under the number 9.477.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will only ask you whether you can recognise some names which are mentioned or listed in this record of autopsies and identification of bodies from Prhovo mass grave. Can you have a look at the body number 1? Can you read the name? And the whereabouts of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Jusic Osman from the village of Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where did you see him for the last time alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I do not remember, but I just know that this man was killed. I saw him actually there when we were pushing the car. That's where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is the last time where you saw him alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the same person you -- about whom you stated that he was killed when you were returning back to the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. Someone called him Osme and others in the village called him Osman but it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the body number 24? Can you read the name and the date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: It's difficult to see. I assume this is Hadzic Hasim, son of Hajro, born on the 12th of January, 1950. And then I cannot see the other number. It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will try to provide you with better copy. Is it the same or is it better?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Better, it's better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you please read it once again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Hadzic, Hasim, son of Hajro, born on the 21st -- on the 12th of January, 1958.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you saw this person for the last time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: He was killed in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the person who was called out shortly after you were gathered in front of this Karanfil Osmanovic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want you to have a look at the body number 30. And can you please read the name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Hamdija Islamagic son of Pasa born on the 1st of November, 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see this man last time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I saw him for the last time when he was dragged into Prhovo by a truck. He was dragged on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I just -- you had the opportunity to see this exhumation report or better say identification record yesterday. You were able to see, for example, the names under number 3 and 4. If you can have a look at the body number 3 and 4, you can see that there are names of two females. Do you know these females or better say did you know these two women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they from -- or were they from the village of Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it when you saw them for the last time alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: When we were in the column altogether. Then we went to Peci so I guess they were killed later but we found them when we opened up the graves. We found their bodies in the graves -- in the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time when you left Prhovo for Peci, these people were alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you agree, I wouldn't go through each and every name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you confirm that these people in this record were killed either in the village of Prhovo or on the road from Prhovo to Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, is it the first time you're seeing this document or have you seen it before? Has it been shown to you before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have had an opportunity to go through it page after page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show the witness two other records on exhumation and identification. It will be Exhibit number P1108, and P1109, the disclosure number is 9.478 and 9.479 respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is exhumation from the year 1999. Are you aware of the fact that there was second exhumation in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this record, it is said that mass grave was located in the place called sick Ciganska Dolina; is it correct? Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to read only one sentence from this report, and I am talking about the report -- I'm sorry, because we were -- I mentioned two exhibit numbers so now I'm talking about Exhibit number P1108. And I want to read on the second page, the last-but-one paragraph and it says, "The bodies were then marked in the order of the exhumation starting from number 1." Can you see it? In fact what I am reading it is already in the middle of this paragraph, the paragraph itself starts with the words [B/C/S spoken]. And in the middle, it says, "On body number 4, a rectangular flashlight was found while body number 6 had no footwear. After body number 7, a grey, long-sleeved men's jumper was found into which four pairs of mostly rubber boots had been crammed. And then again, body number 9 had no footwear." Do you remember stating that when you stop at the field near to the Peci, you were ordered to take out -- take off your shoes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we assume that these persons who were marked as body number 6 and 9, might have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I object to what we can assume might have been. That's not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stated in your statement that in the field near the Peci, you were ordered to take your shoes off and then you stated that some men were killed on that spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you have a look at the Exhibit number P1109? And on the page number 2 is a list of people who were exhumed and identified in this mass grave. You were able to see this list yesterday. Can you say whether the people who are listed here were together with you on the road in the column from Prhovo to Peci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I didn't know if they were all in the column, because I wasn't allowed to look, but I know that they were found later in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the number 8?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Ismet Mesic, son of Emsud born on the 16th of March, 1977, Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this guy one of them who were -- who you stated was killed as the youngest of you when only 14 of you remained after the shooting in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: He was the youngest as well as Senad Hadzic. The two of them were the youngest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see Senad Hadzic's name under number 12 and his date of born was 1st February, 1976. My last question, which you already answered during the examining the document -- the first document, Exhibit P947, was there any resistance in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any military resistance in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Just one not exactly a question but a remark that I would like. If you -- if you have a look at this last document, 9.479, halfway down the page, first paragraph in that part, end of that paragraph, it says, "The Kljuc PU will compile special records on the identification of the bodies." Do you have that record, that document? Is it available?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have to check this information with our in-house expert on exhumations. To my knowledge, I didn't find this record, but it is possible that he received this information. I'm sorry, but we will deal with exhumation at a later point, so I am sure that all these documents will be discussed again and in more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman? Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is the lead counsel for the accused Radoslav Brdjanin and he will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Sir, are you aware that on May 19th, 1992, there was an order for the JNA to evacuate Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any JNA units leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina, passing near your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke this morning, and I want to start with the 26th of May, 1992. You spoke about hearing gunfire. You saw men from your village being escorted and you said in your statement, your second statement to the Prosecutor, which was dated 21 July, 2001, you said, "I would estimate that there were four or five Serb soldiers. They were wearing masks over their head. I would describe these masks as both black ski masks and others were wearing women's stockings over their faces." That was your statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why is it you have to estimate there were four or five Serb soldiers involved? Did you see them or did you not see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
