utterances.text: I saw two, Brankovic and Milanko Popovic in the village, and when I came from the woods, back into the village, there were many soldiers there, not two, three or four or five. I saw these two of -- two soldiers who came with these men of ours who had gone there to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me re-ask the question. In your statement to the Prosecutor, in 2001, you said this, and I quote exactly what the statement says you said, "I would estimate that there were four or five Serb soldiers. They were wearing masks over their head. I would describe these masks as both black ski mask and others were wearing women's stockings over their faces." Now that's the statement I'm referring to. Did you see these four or five soldiers that you're speaking of in that statement? Did you yourself see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I saw many more than these four or five. I knew Milanko Popovic and Branko Brankovic personally. And we were on good terms before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already know that and you've already told us that. My question is: Did you personally see these four or five that you referred to in your statement in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I've told you, not four. There were many more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your statement of 2001 incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: All the statements are correct in my opinion, they are all correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All your statements are correct, all the ones you made to the OTP? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described these soldiers as people who were wearing masks over their faces so you could not see their faces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people who were wearing masks over their faces who you could not see, you did not know their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: How do I know they were Serbs? A Muslim wouldn't attack Muslims and the Muslims in the village didn't have weapons. It was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I know because there were civilians bearing weapons and there were also soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were soldiers? Because they were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes. They had JNA camouflage uniforms on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I know because I served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were they JNA uniforms or did they just look like JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: They looked the same as those in the JNA, same colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told all the time to keep your head down so you weren't able to really examine those uniforms very carefully, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Only if you would peep around a little, because there were soldiers around us all the time watching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that during the war in 1992, many civilians put on uniforms who were not soldiers? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I do know, but who gave them those uniforms, then? Where did they get them from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well do you know the answer to the question you just asked me? Do you know who gave them the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they got them from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. I wasn't involved in politics. I was a man in -- living in a village, farming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers you saw, that were all wearing masks or stockings over their faces, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I saw Milanko and Branko Brankovic. Those two, the two I knew them, and they weren't wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about them. I'm asking you about the ones that were wearing masks and stockings over their faces. Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was their commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The second time when they came, I heard this from people who knew him, it was Marko Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't know Marko Adamovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered that question in chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only thing you know about Marko Adamovic is what somebody else told you, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that? Who told you that person was Marko Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: People who knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me a name. Who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I'd rather not mention the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask the Court to order to you mention the name of who told you that this person was Marko Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If the Court will give the order that we should go to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We go in private session first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to acknowledge that he heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we go into open session, I said. Yes Mr. Ackerman proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd just like the witness to acknowledge what you just told him. That he heard it and understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard me and understood me, haven't you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you do promise not to discuss this portion of your evidence with those two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago you told us that everything you said in your two statements to the OTP is correct, right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave in the first statement you gave to the OTP was in 1997 and the second one you gave to the OTP was in 2001. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 2001, you mentioned that you needed to correct something that was incorrect in your previous statement. You said that in your previous statement, you mentioned that the next day, the Serbs came to collect weapons from our village. This was a mistake, they came on the same day. So at least one of the statements in your first statement, you have acknowledged was incorrect, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. The Serbs collected weapons twice. First the people who were in the village surrendered their weapons and the second time, people who were not in the village, who were in hiding in their houses, in their basements and so on. So they came to collect weapons twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not correct, then, when you said in your 2001 statement, and I'm going to quote what you said. "In my previous statement I mentioned that the next day, the Serbs came to collect weapons from our village. This was a mistake. The Serbs arrived in our village to collect the weapons on the same day of the negotiations not the next day." Is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The Serbs came to collect weapons twice. The first day and later on, when they killed people, when the population was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the whole point is very simple one. I mean, you could answer the question which was clear enough. Okay. You are saying that there were two occasions when the Serbs came to collect weapons. Forget the second of these two occasions. And stick to the first. Did the Serbs arrive in your village to collect weapons on the first occasion on the same day of the negotiations or the day before -- or the day after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the negotiations were conducted, they came to collect weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got your answer, Mr. Ackerman, and that's it. So when you basically the day before -- or on the occasion before, and the first statement said that they had come to collect the weapons, the day after the negotiations, was that a correct presentation of the facts or an incorrect one? Did you make a mistake at that time, which you corrected afterwards, or have we misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago. I can remember the main events. I've already forgotten the details. I can't remember each and every detail from the beginning to the end. It's many years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that we understand but any way, can we move to the next question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, it's kind of a follow-up of what we've been talking about, you have agreed that in your initial statement of August, 1997, you mentioned that the Serbs came to collect weapons the next day. Four years later, when you gave your second statement, you realised that that statement in the -- in 1997 was a mistake. How is it that you realised that you had made that mistake? Did someone tell you that it was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no. No one told me. I can't remember every single day, every minute. It's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think your memory may have been better five years after the event than it was nine years after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I remembered better years ago rather than ten years later. I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now talk about Branko Brankovic and Milanko Popovic. You've said these are soldiers that you recognised because they weren't wearing masks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those two soldiers, how long had they been in the army? If you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What army was it they were in, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't know which army they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they had been stationed before they showed up in your village, what base they were stationed at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who their commander was? Would you say it's this same person, Adamovic that you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: The second time it was Marko Adamovic. The first time, I don't know who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Adamovic's commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what military unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers that were all in -- had their faces covered and had stockings over their heads and all of those things, you've told us that you don't know where they were from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I ask you that question, if you know where they were from, I'm including places like Macedonia, Serbia, all of former Yugoslavia. You don't know where in the former Yugoslavia these people were from, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No. I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know if the soldiers you saw the first time were the same soldiers you saw the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I don't because I didn't see their faces. I couldn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for just a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interviewed in 2001, did you have an opportunity to read your statement from 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't read in 2001 your previous statement and you didn't make the correction based on the previous statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember, but I did provide statements on several occasions. I gave a statement in Kljuc, I gave a statement in Croatia. I gave a statement in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave the statement to the investigator of ICTY, from ICTY in 2001, did he give you your previous statement to read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT-77
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two or three statements? The record doesn't reflect it but I'm told what he said was he made two or three statements in Kljuc and one in Croatia and one in Slovenia. Does the Prosecution have these statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we weren't informed on any statement made in Croatia and I think the statement he refers to as the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just answer the question. Do you have or have you ever had in your possession as Office of the Prosecutor, in other words, any other statement made by this person, by this witness, elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No we did not have. We have a ruling that Nedzad Jusic was confirmed dead, and he gave a statement probably to Lower Court in Kljuc but we do not have any other statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that declaration, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied it's the case they don't have the statements. I'm a little concerned about why. I assume this witness had told them at one other point that he has made such statements. I think they should have tried to get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can equally assume the opposite that he never told hem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that -- sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony. You are free to go. Once more, I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of everyone for having accepted to come over here and give evidence in this trial. Thank you, you will now be escorted out of the courtroom, and may I just remind you not to discuss any of the points that you testified upon with any other person, especially persons that you may think may be coming over here to give evidence? I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the other witness in line?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have a motion now that the witness has gone. I move that his testimony -- entire testimony be stricken on the grounds that he was unable to identify the alleged soldiers, where they were from, who they were commanded by, or anything that would tie to the allegations contained in the indictment regarding the -- well, regarding anything, the indictment simply does -- there is no way to tie his testimony to Mr. Brdjanin in any way because he doesn't know who the soldiers were. They could have been from Macedonia, they could have been from Serbia, they could have been from anywhere. They are not tied to any organisation that's part of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a witness who will be accepted according to Rule 92 who corroborates his statement. We have his testimony that he recognised two men from this -- among these people. We have the testimony that he is sure that who was his commander, and we have lots of documents which tied this person with Kljuc area and mopping up operations in Kljuc area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, what I suggest we do is so that we don't waste time on this moment, that you table a motion properly, formally, in writing, and we will deal with it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think probably the logical way, Your Honour, is maybe at the close of the Prosecutor's case, when I file that motion of no case to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can act -- you are free to file a motion at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to restrict you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Equally what Madam Richterova has just stated might -- either reinforce your conviction to file the motion or convince you of the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It probably makes more sense to formalise it after we've heard all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However it goes in the record that you have this intention in mind. Next question -- next witness. Unfortunately, could you contact my secretary, please? Because I had figured out that this witness will be coming after the next break. So I left the -- his statements downstairs in my Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour before the next witness is brought in, I have to inform the Court that Ms. Korner will be here at 1.30 to address Your Honours on the matter that Mr. Ackerman wanted to raise in her presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would 15 minutes be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably not, but we can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will try. So I give you five and five each, ten minutes, and then five additional minutes to round it up. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour the next witness is witness 7.155, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness's name is Samir Dedic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dedic. You know that you've come here to this Tribunal to give evidence in this trial and because of that, I need to inform you that in terms of the rules, before we proceed with hearing your testimony, I must ask you to make, to enter a solemn declaration to tell us the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration in your own language is -- appears on the sheet of paper that the usher is going to give you now. May I kindly ask you to proceed by reading that declaration aloud? That would be your solemn undertaking to this Tribunal that you will be telling us the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down. Yes. Mr. Dedic, calm down. You don't need to get nervous. Everyone will be treating you nicely in here. Let me explain to you first of all who we are. Three of us here is -- I am the Presiding Judge in this trial and I am flanked on my right by Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and to my left Judge Taya from Japan. We will be deciding this case, the case which the Prosecutor has instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin. The procedure here is a very simple one and it's taken in stages. You will first be asked a series of questions in what we refer to as direct examination or examination-in-chief, by the Prosecution, by the Prosecution. Usually it's one officer of the Prosecution -- of the Office of the Prosecutor that conducts the examination-in-chief. This particular occasion, it's Ms. Ann Sutherland who you see to your right standing up. Eventually, when the examination-in-chief is over, then you will be asked questions by the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin. And the Defence team is at your left. The three persons in the front row and I will tell you later who will be amongst them the one to cross-examine you. You are here to speak the truth and therefore it is irrelevant who puts the questions to you. You have to treat and you need to treat the Prosecution and the Defence the same. They both have a right to question you and in each case, in either case, you have a duty to tell us the truth. You will be protected in case there are any questions that you should not be asked or that may potentially harass you unduly. In the meantime, keep calm and my advice to you is to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. If you tell us long stories, it will get you no where. It will help only to complicate matters and will lead you into further questions and more questions and a never-ending series of questions. Ms. Sutherland, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic can you state your full name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Samir Dedic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 1st of October, 1974, in the Kljuc town, in the Kljuc Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father's name is Raif?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were raised in a small Muslim village of Crljeni [Realtime transcript read in error "Soljeni"]?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this village is situated on a hill top about 13 kilometres north of the town of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you lived there with your mother and your younger brother and sister?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, your father had been working in Germany since 1990?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: 17 and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Depends which part of 1992, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May, 1992, you were 17 and a half years old?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were attending school at the Kljuc high school as a third-year chemistry student, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is you are ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you practise a religion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are now married with two small children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you work in the house building industry?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I'm currently unemployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in June, 2001, and you signed a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in September, 2001, you signed a declaration making some corrections to this statement?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't provided a statement to any other authorities concerning the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning back to 1992, approximately how many people lived in the village of Crljeni?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: About 350 villagers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in the village?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military installations or facilities in the village?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the main industry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume it will be corrected in the future but the village is not Sojeni, I don't think, I think it's C-R-L-J-E-N-I; is that correct am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are correct I haven't been following the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a point taken and I'm sure the correction will be made in due course. Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, in 1992, was the main industry in Crljeni agriculture -- agriculture and livestock?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Agriculture and livestock for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you last attend school in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Mid-May, perhaps the last day was maybe the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was school discontinued?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Simply it was dangerous to continue to go to school. The buses weren't working any more and it was an emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at school, how many teachers were of Muslim ethnicity, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but there were perhaps four or five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many teachers were of Serb ethnicity, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the Muslim teachers stopped coming to school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not all at once but gradually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why this was so?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I found out just that they were not allowed to attend the teachers' staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Serb teachers treat the Muslim children, the Muslim pupils? Any differently from the Serb children?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I noticed some changes in the way they behaved. They viewed us differently, us pupils, from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn your mind to the end of May, 1992. Do you recall what happened in your village at the end of May?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: This happened on the 26th of May, when the whole village moved to the other side of the Sana River to the village of Plamenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason that the whole village moved to Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Because we heard a man was working in some woods just outside of the village, and he noticed soldiers, and he came to the village in a panic and he said that they were going to attack the village, that the Serb army were going to -- was going to attack the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these Serb soldiers captured or arrested?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir you mentioned that the whole village moved to Plamenica, how far away is that from the village of Crljeni?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: This is a little more difficult, because the Sana River crosses that road so you have to go to Kljuc first and that is 26 kilometres away, so it's much faster just to cross the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the crow flies, from Crljeni to Plamenica, approximately how far is it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: About one kilometre, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else stay behind in Crljeni?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Some elderly people who were not able to leave stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the persons who lived in the village of Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: The place where we came to, Muslims were there, but there were some Serb hamlets there also.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1097?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, if you could take a moment to orient yourself with that map? Then if you could take a pointer beside you and point to the village of Crljeni?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the village of Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned there is a river running between the two.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you I've finished with the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that evening after you arrived in Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were put up in the houses of relatives and friends and that's how we spent the night, with constant shooting and fear. It was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was shooting, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Serb soldiers and paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these Serb soldiers and paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Not at night, but it was dangerous to look out of the window or to go outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them the following day?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could see them through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going it to request a clarification. In 71, line 3, the transcript reflects that the witness answered Serb soldiers and paramilitary forces. There is some indication that what he might have said was Serb soldiers who were paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you heard what Mr. Ackerman has just remarked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was your answer to Ms. Sutherland's question? The question was who was shooting, if you know? What did you actually answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Serb soldiers and paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these soldiers the following day?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that you could see them through the windows, from the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, olive-drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they -- were you able to see any insignia on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Mostly on their sleeves, the Serbian flag, the four letters "S".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the village of Plamenica for?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Until the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, was any property damaged?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: The houses were torched, a lot of the houses were knocked down, barns were torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody being mistreated during these three days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but we weren't -- we didn't dare to leave the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. Would you like to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. That's why I'm looking in your direction. So we'll have a 25 minute break, resuming immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Ms. Sutherland continues, may I just apologise, I'm afraid the court was kept waiting because I was given a whole lot of stuff by Mr. Ackerman at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No need to apologise. Ms. Sutherland, would you proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, before we had a short break, we were dealing with events in the village of Plamenica. Do you know a man by the name of Hamdo Islamagic?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to know of this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I learnt later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I heard that that was his name, that he is from that village of Plamenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that gentleman being mistreated at all in the village of Plamenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I saw him tied to a truck or an armoured vehicle and he was being dragged along the road. He was dead probably. He was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Hamdo dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: He had a shirt and trousers but they were already 50 per cent torn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After three days in the village of Plamenica, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I joined the other men from our village of Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you by yourself or were you with others?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: There were another two or three young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these young men --

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Also under age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the names and ages of these young men that were with you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Fahrudin Omerovic. He was also born in 1974 like I was and, Ermin Dedic, also he was 17 and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Esad Kablic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, he was born in 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he with you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you and these other young men went to join the men from the village of Crljeni. Where were the other men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They were on the edge of the forest, close to the village of Plamenica, simply they were hiding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, how many, approximately how many men were there in this group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Between 70 and 80 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, did this group come out of the woods?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened when you joined them in the woods?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: A man by the name of Milovan Djukic, whose house was in the Sana River valley, and it belonged to hamlet of Ninici, he called on the men to surrender voluntarily, that nothing would happen to them and that they would be allowed to go it to their homes. However, quite the opposite was true and we all know where we ended up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these men armed in your group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: When I joined the group, when I reached the group, I heard from the other men who were there that five men had already been called to bring down the weapons, those five of them, so that I didn't see anyone with weapons when I arrived, because those men had already left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many weapons these five men had taken from the group of approximately 70 or 80 men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already said there were eight or nine hunting rifles and one or two pistols, one of which was my father's, and he had a regular licence for that hunting rifle. However, it was seized from him and it was never returned to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the men came to the house of Milovan Djukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the two villages of Crljeni and Plamenica, was that in the valley in between these two villages, by the river?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Quite right. 50 metres from the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Milovan Djukic's occupation was before the war?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: He had a store and a cafe, restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you got to the house?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: We had to walk with our hands behind our heads, and we had to look down so that we couldn't see much but I did see quite a number of soldiers and armoured vehicles, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were there, did you see?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: In my estimate, about a hundred soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the group of 70 or 80 men when you arrived at the house?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: As soon as we arrived, we reached the house, they started mistreating individual men. There was a fence there, a kind of warehouse, storage space, and they put us up there. We were there for about 15 minutes. We had hoped that we would be going home. However, I saw two buses arriving from the direction of Kljuc and then I assumed that they were intended for us, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment. Did you recognise any of these men at the house?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court the names of the people that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: My teacher, Slobodan Ninic, who was my teacher in elementary school. Then the school principal from Sokolovo, Boro Pesevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Slobodan Ninic dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: He was wearing jeans and on top he had a camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: He was sitting on a chair and he had a rifle over his shoulder and as we arrived, each one of us stood next to him and he took down the data, our personal data, name, surname, date of birth, and then we passed by him and entered this area with the fence round it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ninic and Pesevic aware that you were under age?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at that point in time, they didn't want to acknowledge it. That is what I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had -- were you taught by Slobodan Ninic at school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was quite a long time ago, up to fourth grade of primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after your names had been written down?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: We sat down. They escorted us to this fenced-in area and that is where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some buses had arrived from the -- from Kljuc. Were they civilian or military buses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Civilian buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any insignia on the buses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: There were the markings of the public enterprise Sana Kljuc. Those were the words written on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you put -- were you placed on the buses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: About 15 minutes later, they told us to get into the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: First they took us to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: The bus stopped and during the whole journey, we had to keep our hands behind our heads and our heads bowed between our knees throughout the trip, so that we only saw where we were once we arrived. It was on the main road between the municipality building and the elementary school in front of the entrance to the elementary school in Kljuc. That is where the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: From the bus, I saw a large number of soldiers in town already. There were few civilians to be seen. Then they ordered us to get up, but still with our hands behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: There were various uniforms, camouflage, blue uniforms, police uniforms, olive-grey uniforms, and en route to Kljuc, there were three armed soldiers in the bus with their guns pointed at us, who threatened if anybody were to raise their heads they would shoot immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers wearing red berets?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Not then but before, yes. While I was still going to school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see these people that were wearing red berets?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: In town, walking around and shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where these soldiers were from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I learnt and heard that they had come from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: The other students, citizens, the people of Kljuc, that was the information going around, because we hadn't -- we didn't use to see them before so they must have come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately when was the first time you saw these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: At the end of May, or rather the end of April and the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can return now to when you got off the bus, when you arrived Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at the school, what was the name of the school again?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Nikola Mackic elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They ordered us to get up with our hands behind our heads, and to get off the bus slowly. In the meantime, those soldiers were hitting the windows of the buses, threatening to slaughter us, to kill us, so that this was unbelievable fear that we were in. Everything was so strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: As we were getting off, on the steps, still on the steps, there were soldiers on both sides, so that whoever got off was -- received a blow on the head or somewhere else but in any event he would be beaten. And from the road to the school itself, it's about 50 metres, so they formed this gauntlet, two lines of soldiers on either side and we had to pass in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you ran through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: It was terrible. We were being beaten from all sides. No one could avoid it. The path we ran over was covered in blood as with the tip of their rifles, they would hit many people, which caused bleeding and the path was all in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you hit?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: This was slow, you see, the way we passed took time because at the entrance to the building, everyone had to lean his hands against the wall and then he would be searched so that the beating lasted sometime, until the person at the entrance was being searched and deprived of everything he had on his -- a watch or a chain or anything else. This would be seized and once they finished with him, then they would take care of the next one and the person would be allowed to go into the corridors where the beating would continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What building were you taken to after you were searched?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: It was the sports hall, the gym, the gym, where we had physical education in school. Did you ask me where we were searched?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You were searched outside before you were taken into the building. I understand.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: At the entrance, yes, at the entrance, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were inside the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: It was packed full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, maybe some Croats because there were some Croats in Kljuc. There was a certain percentage of Croats too. But mostly, they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you questioned about?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They would kick one in the back, somebody in the back, and tell him to get up, and then they would take him to three or four premises that existed, and they would take him inside and they would ask us to confess things that we had never dreamed of. Many people had to confess because of the torture and mistreatment. They had to confess things that were not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your questioning, were you asked how old you were?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, not in the room but at the entrance, yes, the soldier -- a soldier was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How tall were you then and how much did you weigh?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: One metre 70, and I had over 60 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in the Nikola Mackic elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: We got there in the evening, about 4.00, and until the next day at 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, were you provided with any food?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't get anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time were you told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No. We spent the time sitting down all the time with our hands on our backs and it was really dreadful. They would just pass in between the lines and kick one or two or hit people in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you stayed there until the next day at 7.00 p.m. in the evening. Where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Again, they boarded us on the buses. They didn't tell us where they were taking us. During the journey, again, they threatened if anyone raised his head, they would shoot, and they frightened us. They said they were taking us for execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people dressed, the men on the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: They stopped the bus again we didn't know where we were, but we saw that later. We got off, and again there was a sports hall there, and this locality is called Sitnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the Sitnica elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Six or seven days, six or seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men and boys were in the school gym?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: As many as in Kljuc. We were all transferred there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided food in this place of detention?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of food were you provided?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: It was like a sandwich, but really small, a little piece of bread and some salami.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you called out for questioning at the Sitnica school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any other people that were called out for questioning?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. This was just a transit point on the way to the Manjaca camp so that there wasn't much interrogation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: He was a teacher in -- a teacher of history in the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Sitnica elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Did he say that he was -- did he just say that he was a teacher, a teacher of history in the secondary school or did he also say that he was his teacher? Was he your teacher? Because I heard you say "moj" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in the school and he taught me history for two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Omer Filipovic being called out for questioning?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR DEDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him being called out there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm about to move to another topic and we were going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we can stop here. Mr. Dedic, we need to stop here because there is a procedural point that we need to take up, about which you have nothing to do, it doesn't concern you, so you will be escorted out of this courtroom and that will be all for today. You will be returning to this courtroom tomorrow morning and we will take it up from there and hopefully by tomorrow it, you will be finished. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to respect it to five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into it private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
